analysis.one_liner: Requires states to flag salvage, rebuilt, and flood damage on car titles so buyers know a car's history.
analysis.headline: Passed the Senate unanimously and the House 271-133, but the two chambers never agreed on a final version before Congress ended, so it never became law.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created one national standard for car titles. Wrecked, rebuilt, junked, and flood-damaged cars would carry that history on the title forever, sellers of rebuilt salvage cars would have to tell buyers in writing and put a label on the windshield, and a national database would instantly show whether a car had ever been branded salvage. It also made it a federal offense to forge titles, fake inspections, or haul a car across state lines to dodge the branding rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Buyers of used and rebuilt cars. Today a wrecked car can be repaired, shipped to a state with loose rules, and retitled with no sign of its past. The bill would have required every participating state to carry salvage, rebuilt, junk, and flood branding forward on every title, made sellers hand buyers a written disclosure before a rebuilt salvage car changes hands, and let a buyer instantly check a vehicle identification number against the national title database. Honest dealers and insurers would also benefit from a level playing field against sellers who hide a car's damage history.

how_it_helps.text: Each state would have to print prior salvage, rebuilt, junk, nonrepairable, or flood branding on every new title for a car, along with the state that issued the original branded title, so a damaged car's history follows it across state lines.

A seller of a rebuilt salvage vehicle would have to give the buyer a written disclosure before the sale, and a tamper-resistant label would have to stay on the car's windshield or window until the first retail purchaser takes delivery.

The National Motor Vehicle Title Information System would have to let a user instantly find out whether a car, or a car with a given vehicle identification number, has ever been reported as salvage, rebuilt salvage, or nonrepairable.

Selling a salvage or nonrepairable vehicle as rebuilt, forging titles and inspection certificates, falsifying inspection results, and moving cars in interstate commerce to escape titling rules would all be unlawful, with civil penalties up to $2,000 per vehicle and state attorneys general empowered to sue on behalf of residents.

Cars acquired by insurance companies through total-loss settlements would automatically require salvage titles, closing a common route by which badly damaged cars reenter the market with clean titles.

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the costs would fall on auto insurers, which would have to obtain salvage titles and notify owners after total-loss settlements; on salvage yards, rebuilders, and sellers of rebuilt vehicles, who would face inspections, documentation of replacement parts, disclosure duties, and penalties; and on state titling agencies, which would have to overhaul their title systems, though a federal report would explore whether user fees could cover those costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, salvage yards, and state agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill would preempt state titling laws in participating states, overriding state definitions of salvage, flood, and related terms and state titling and inspection procedures, though states could keep stricter damage thresholds and could make additional disclosures.

Enforcement would run through state chief law enforcement officers rather than private lawsuits, with a civil penalty capped at $2,000 per vehicle and a two-year time limit, so buyers hurt by a hidden wreck would have no new federal claim of their own.

Disclosure obligations only apply when the seller has actual knowledge of the flood damage or rebuilt salvage status, and the bill states that making the required disclosure does not create liability for the vehicle's condition or reduced value — weakening the protection for buyers who are still deceived.

A flood vehicle could escape the 'Flood' brand if an insurance adjuster or dealer inspection finds no water-damaged electrical or mechanical components, and no such inspection is required unless the owner or insurer is trying to avoid the brand.

States would bear the cost of new uniform title standards, inspections, and secure decals and documents; the Secretary of Transportation would only have to report on whether user fees or forfeited law-enforcement money could cover them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For used-car buyers the bill offered a real fix to a well-documented problem: cars totaled in wrecks or floods being rebuilt and resold with titles that hide their history. The main compromises an honest supporter would acknowledge are that the disclosure rules lean on what a seller actually knew, the penalties are modest, and federal preemption replaces some state rules with a national floor that is not always higher. On balance the consumer protections outweigh those costs, which is why the bill drew broad bipartisan sponsorship and unanimous Senate approval.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed its own amended version 271-133 on October 10, 1998, but the Senate never voted on that House version before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, so the bill died without a final agreement.

narrative.text: Sen. Trent Lott introduced the bill on June 9, 1997, and it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee; 57 senators — 17 Democrats and 40 Republicans — signed on as cosponsors.
The Commerce Committee held hearings on September 25, 1997, ordered the bill reported favorably on November 4, 1997, and reported it with a substitute amendment on July 27, 1998.
The Senate passed the bill with an amendment by unanimous consent on October 2, 1998.

On October 10, 1998, the House passed the bill as amended under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure, which requires a two-thirds vote; the tally was 271 to 133 with 2 present, with Republicans voting 205-1 in favor and Democrats 66-131 against.
The House's amended version was messaged back to the Senate on October 12, 1998, but the Senate never took it up, and the bill expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers of rebuilt, salvage, and flood-damaged vehicles, along with the salvage and insurance businesses around them, kept operating under a patchwork of state rules with no national title branding, and used-car buyers kept bearing the risk of buying a wrecked or flooded car with a clean-looking title.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sellers of rebuilt and flood-damaged cars

sides.party_line_note: The bill had heavy bipartisan sponsorship — 17 Democrats and 40 Republicans in the Senate — and passed the Senate by unanimous consent, but on the House floor the vote split sharply: Republicans 205-1 for, Democrats 66-131 against.

industries.note: The bill would require insurers to obtain salvage titles and give notice after total-loss settlements, but it also shields anyone making the required disclosure from liability for the car's condition and lets an insurance adjuster's inspection clear a car of the 'Flood' brand, so insurers gain a uniform national system along with their duties.

The bill would lock in a legal rebuilt-salvage market with defined titles, anti-theft and safety inspections, and door-jamb decals, while imposing new documentation, inspection, and disclosure costs on the businesses that rebuild and resell wrecked cars.

Dealers would have to give written flood and rebuilt-salvage disclosures before selling, but the carry-forward branding and instant national title checks would also protect honest dealers from unknowingly buying and reselling branded cars.
